sources.text:
Iran launched an attack on Bahrain early Sunday, the latest strike on the kingdom, as clashes between Iran and the U.S. continue while peace talks remain stalled. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said it targeted radar positions at Bahrain’s Riffa Air Base with six drones. Jordan, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and Qatar all strongly condemned the attack and expressed solidarity with Bahrain. Bahrain is officially home to the U.S. Navy’s Fifth Fleet, though the Pentagon largely abandoned its base there after it was heavily damaged by Iranian attacks in the opening days of the U.S. war on Iran. In recent weeks, U.S. forces have quietly hit several Iranian targets, among them Qeshm Island, which houses a major Revolutionary Guard naval facility. This is Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson.
Esmail Baghaei: “We will not leave any attack unanswered. No military aggression against Iran by the United States or others will go unanswered. We have demonstrated this in practice, and we will continue to act in the future in whatever manner and by whatever means Iran’s powerful armed forces deem appropriate.”

sources.news_title: Iran's Revolutionary Guard Sends 6 Drones at US Radar Site in Bahrain, Ending a Lull in Gulf Attacks
sources.text:
Iran launched a drone attack against a military base in Bahrain, its second strike on the country in the past three days.
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it used six drones to target the U.S. air defense radar facility at al-Riffa air base in Bahrain on Sunday, days after similarly firing drones at Bahrain on Friday, according to the BBC.
The strikes break a two-month lull in Iranian attacks on Gulf states, testing fragile peace negotiations aimed at ending the eight-month conflict and reopening the Strait of Hormuz, which is a crucial global oil supply channel. The strait remains severely restricted in a dual standoff: the U.S. Navy blockades Iranian ports while Iran enforces permit rules, cutting traffic roughly 65%.
"The U.S. air defense radar system at the Al-Riffa helicopter base in Bahrain was targeted by six drones belonging to the IRGC Aerospace Force," the IRGC said in a statement posted by the state broadcaster on Telegram, cited by CBS News.
Bahrain's military told the BBC its air defense systems intercepted and destroyed the drones "before they could achieve their objectives".
Bahrain's foreign ministry told the broadcaster: "The Kingdom of Bahrain condemns in the strongest terms the continued brutal Iranian attacks on its territory and holds Iran fully responsible for their consequences."
Al-Riffa Air Base hosts critical U.S. air defense infrastructure, including a key U.S. early-warning air defense radar site, and supports American rotary-wing operations.
Bahrain is home to the U.S. Navy’s 5th Fleet, making the installation a high-priority strategic asset amid ongoing regional tensions near the Strait of Hormuz.
The U.S. Embassy in Bahrain on Sunday warned Americans to exercise “heightened vigilance,” adding that there could be possible flight cancellations, airspace closures and other travel disruptions after the drone attacks, CNN reported.
Friday's Attack as Iran War Continues
The U.S. military said it intercepted two Iranian attack drones headed toward Bahrain on Sunday, while the IRGC claimed it struck a U.S. early warning radar system in the kingdom. The U.S. denied Iran's claim.
Last week, officials moved U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent from his Washington D.C. home to a military base over alleged threats to his life from Iran. Other U.S. officials, like Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, also occupy base housing.
On Monday, Iran's state broadcaster, citing Tehran's Navy, said a tanker east of the Strait of Hormuz had caught fire after hitting a naval mine.
It said the ship was traveling through a "restricted area," which "exposes offending vessels to serious risks," according to CBS News.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi also said that a 10-nation regional bloc had backed Iran's plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days if the U.S. agrees to a ceasefire and meets seven conditions.
But so far, the Trump administration has rejected Iran's demands to ease economic sanctions on the country.

The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said six drones targeted “the US air defence radar system at the Al-Riffa helicopter base in Bahrain,” calling the strike the second phase of its response to hostile US actions. “Any aggression by the American enemy will be met with an even harsher and more forceful response,” the Guards said in a statement carried by Iranian state television, according to AFP. The IRGC released footage of the launches:
The general command of the Bahrain Defence Force said “Iran continues its systematic hostile approach through its sinful attacks targeting the Kingdom of Bahrain” (translated), and that its air defenses intercepted the drones before they reached their targets. There were no immediate reports of injuries or damage.

The Interior Ministry put out two nationwide alerts, Bahrain’s first since September, telling citizens and residents to “remain calm, proceed to the nearest safe location”:
Bahrain’s Foreign Ministry said the kingdom “rejects turning its territory into an arena for settling scores and holds Iran fully responsible” for the attacks on Friday and Sunday and their consequences, RFE/RL reported.
On Friday, the Guards claimed they had destroyed a US early-warning radar in Bahrain in retaliation for American strikes on a telecommunications tower in Sirik, in southern Iran, as we reported. Saudi Arabia condemned the attacks on Bahrain as a violation of international law. Its own air defenses intercepted two ballistic missiles that Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis fired at Riyadh, along with drones over the Eastern Province. Tehran has been widening the map: Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, warned this week that if American aircraft use bases in Europe to attack Iran, “we may even target some US military bases in European countries.”

sources.news_title: Bahrain Intercepts Iranian Drone Attack as Gulf Tensions Return
sources.text:
Iran says six drones targeted a U.S. radar installation, but neither Bahrain nor Washington has confirmed that the facility was hit
Bahrain said its air defences intercepted several Iranian drone attacks on Sunday, ending a relative lull and raising new concerns about a wider return to fighting in the Gulf.
Air-raid sirens sounded across the kingdom, and authorities issued two warnings directing residents to remain calm and move to safe locations. The Bahrain Defence Force said the incoming threats were destroyed before reaching their targets. No casualties or damage were reported.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps gave a different account. It said six drones attacked a U.S. air-defence radar at the Al-Riffa helicopter base. There was no independent confirmation that the radar was struck.
The attack was the second directed at Bahrain in three days. On Friday, the U.S. military said it intercepted two Iranian drones, while Tehran claimed it had struck another early-warning radar. Washington denied that claim and reported no damage.
Bahrain hosts the U.S. Navy’s Fifth Fleet, making the island kingdom an important base for American operations in the Persian Gulf. Its Foreign Ministry accused Iran of trying to turn Bahraini territory into an arena for settling its dispute with the United States.
The renewed attack complicates diplomatic efforts to contain the conflict, which began with U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28. President Donald Trump has recently indicated that further U.S. attacks may not be necessary, but Washington continues to enforce its naval blockade of Iran.
Shipping through the Strait of Hormuz also remains vulnerable. The waterway normally carries about one-fifth of the world’s oil supply, giving any renewed fighting consequences far beyond the region.

Iran launches drone attack on US military base in Bahrain
Iran launched a drone attack on a US military base in Bahrain on Sunday, its second attempt to target the Gulf country in three days, escalating tensions over control of the Strait of Hormuz. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it used six drones to target an air defence radar facility at Al-Riffa air base.
Bahrain’s military said its air defence systems intercepted and destroyed the drones before they could reach their targets. The country’s interior ministry urged residents to move to safe locations as sirens sounded, while its foreign ministry condemned the attacks and held Iran responsible for their consequences.
The latest attack follows an earlier drone assault on Friday, which Iran claimed had damaged a US early warning radar system in Bahrain. The US military denied the claim, saying two Iranian drones were intercepted without causing injuries or damage.
The confrontation comes amid a dispute over the Strait of Hormuz, a strategic shipping route through which about a fifth of global oil and gas supplies normally pass. Iran has restricted shipping and attacked vessels it considers unauthorised, while the US military is escorting tankers to maintain Gulf energy exports. Efforts to reach an agreement to end the war and reopen the strait have stalled, with Donald Trump, US president, saying Washington is no longer interested in a deal.
Israel kills Hamas commander in strike on Gaza displacement camp
Israel has killed Samir Abu Younis, a senior Hamas commander accused of helping plan and oversee the October 7, 2023, attack on Israel, in an airstrike on a displacement camp in Al-Mawasi, southern Gaza, according to Israeli and Palestinian officials.
Younis, 53, who was appointed commander of Hamas’s Rafah Brigade in September, was killed on Saturday. Hamas’s armed wing confirmed his death, while the Israeli military said it had targeted him and taken measures to minimise civilian casualties.
Eyewitnesses said four missiles struck a tent at Al-Waha camp, triggering a fire. A medical source at Nasser Hospital reported that three injured people and one body were brought to the facility.
Israel described Younis as a senior Hamas figure involved in rebuilding the Rafah Brigade and planning attacks against Israeli civilians and troops. Hamas said he joined its armed wing in 1991 and played a major role in planning the October 2023 assault, which killed about 1,200 people in Israel and saw 251 others taken hostage.
The strike comes despite a ceasefire reached in October 2025. Israel says its continued attacks target remaining Hamas militants and are permitted under the agreement. More than 1,640 Palestinians have been killed since the ceasefire, according to Gaza’s health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations.
Zelensky urges US and Musk to lift Starlink restrictions
Volodymyr Zelensky, Ukraine’s president, has urged the United States government and Elon Musk’s SpaceX to lift speed restrictions on Starlink, warning that the limits are weakening the country’s ability to intercept Russian missiles and drones. He said the protection of lives and energy infrastructure ahead of winter depended on restoring the service.
Ukraine uses the standard Starlink network for battlefield communications, while Starlink, a military-grade service controlled by the US government, supports the interception of missiles and drones. Zelensky said interceptor drones lose connection with operators at speeds of about 161 kilometres per hour, making it difficult to pursue faster Russian drones.
The restrictions, first identified in October, have prompted conflicting accounts from Musk and Donald Trump, United States president. Musk said the US government controlled Starshield, while Trump denied responsibility and said he had asked Musk to restore the service.
Zelensky said Ukrainian officials were working with Washington and SpaceX to resolve the issue, adding that the restrictions had political implications because they were being applied in Russian-occupied territories. He urged the parties to be on the “right side of history”.
Megaspeed investigates claims linked to Nvidia chip exports to China
Megaspeed, a Singapore-based technology company and major buyer of Nvidia chips in south-east Asia, has launched an internal investigation following allegations that advanced artificial intelligence chips may have reached Chinese companies despite US export restrictions. The company said it had retained external legal counsel to examine its business, supply chain and global operations.
The investigation follows reports linking Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese spy, to Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s former chief executive, who resigned after allegations of personal relationships involving Alice Huang and an employee emerged. Megaspeed said Alice Huang left her executive role at the company in August 2025.
The company has been suspected of providing Chinese firms with backdoor access to Nvidia chips through data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand. It denied wrongdoing, saying it conducts legitimate and lawful business and that some reports contained claims unsupported by verifiable evidence.
The controversy has also drawn scrutiny from Washington. Scott Bessent, US Treasury secretary, criticised the Commerce Department for failing to act on calls to restrict Megaspeed, while Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has been summoned to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month.
Jordan sentences three men to death over church shooting
A Jordanian court has sentenced three men to death by hanging for a shooting at a Greek Orthodox church in Karak governorate that killed nine people and injured 34 others. The attack occurred on October 23 as mourners attended a Christian funeral at St George’s church in the village of Hmoud.
Jordan’s Armed Forces said the men were convicted of terrorist acts, weapons possession, promoting the ideas of a terrorist organisation and conspiracy to commit terrorist acts. The suspects, two brothers and their brother-in-law, fled the scene but were arrested three days later.
Security footage showed three armed men approaching and firing at the church. The motive for the attack remains unclear, although Karak has a sizeable Christian community in the predominantly Muslim country.
King Abdullah II condemned the shooting and vowed the perpetrators would face the harshest retaliation, saying the attack would not divide Jordanians.
AFRICA
Cape Verde votes in presidential election amid youth emigration concerns
Voters in Cape Verde went to the polls on Sunday to elect a president, with incumbent José Maria Neves facing Rosa, a former justice minister and the country’s first female presidential candidate. The election campaign has centred on job creation and opportunities for young people in the island nation.
The former Portuguese colony, located more than 600 kilometres off the coast of mainland Africa, has about 500,000 residents, while a larger number of Cape Verdeans live abroad, mainly in the United States and Portugal. The country is regarded as one of Africa’s most stable democracies but continues to lose young people seeking employment overseas.
Despite the campaign focus on youth employment, voters in the capital, Praia, reported low enthusiasm among younger people. Some said many young voters were neither motivated nor interested in participating in politics.
Neves, 66, a former prime minister who served for 15 years before becoming president in 2021, is seeking another term. He belongs to the centre-left African Party for the Independence of Cape Verde, which won the legislative elections in May.
UN reports progress in Ebola response but warns of insecurity in Congo
The United Nations has reported progress in efforts to contain an Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo, but warned that rising insecurity is making it harder to reach affected communities. The outbreak, driven by the rare Bundibugyo strain, has recorded more than 11,000 confirmed cases, making it the second-worst Ebola outbreak on record.
Chikwe Ihekweazu, head of the World Health Organization’s Health Emergencies Programme, said infections were declining in former hotspots such as Bunia in eastern Congo. However, new cases were emerging in remote areas where access to healthcare and response teams was more difficult.
He identified insecurity as the biggest obstacle, citing 80 attacks on health facilities and workers. The Bundibugyo strain has no approved vaccine or treatment, adding to the challenges facing medical teams.
Médecins Sans Frontières has criticised the response, saying essential supplies are missing and the virus continues to spread. Julien Harneis, the UN’s special Ebola coordinator, acknowledged the scale of the challenge but said response teams were able to operate across much of the affected region.
Angola seeks 10% stake in De Beers as Botswana backs ownership deal
Angola is seeking a 10 percent stake in De Beers as part of Anglo American’s proposed sale of its majority holding in the diamond producer, according to a spokesperson for the country’s mines ministry. The move would give Angola a share in one of the world’s largest diamond companies as African governments seek greater participation in the industry.
Anglo American put De Beers up for sale in 2024 as part of a wider restructuring, amid falling diamond prices and growing competition from synthetic stones. The company operates mines and exploration projects in Botswana, Namibia, Angola, South Africa and Canada.
Botswana, which held the right of first refusal on Anglo American’s stake, has backed a deal that would increase its ownership of De Beers to 30 percent. President Duma Boko said Namibia and Angola would also participate in the transaction.
Private investors have also expressed interest in the sale, with luxury goods group Richemont among companies reportedly in discussions to join a consortium. The proposed changes could reshape ownership of the diamond producer, giving African governments a larger role in the industry.
AfDB lends Morocco $479m to strengthen climate and energy resilience
The African Development Bank has approved a €434.4 million ($479 million) loan to Morocco to help the country withstand climate and energy-related shocks. The financing, signed with the Moroccan government, is intended to improve the business environment, strengthen climate resilience and encourage private-sector investment.
The programme will support reforms of state-owned enterprises and promote public-private partnerships, particularly in the water and electricity sectors. It will also help Morocco manage the impact of the Middle East crisis, including higher energy and transport costs.
The loan comes as Morocco faces growing pressure to strengthen its infrastructure against climate risks and external energy shocks. The country has experienced severe weather events, including flooding, that have highlighted vulnerabilities in its infrastructure.
Last month, the AfDB added the Moroccan dirham to its financing instruments through its first bond denominated in the currency, worth 1 billion dirhams ($100 million).
Ten killed in Guinea clashes after artisanal mining ban
Ten people, including five foreign nationals, have been killed in clashes between security forces and protesters in Guinea’s northeastern gold-producing region of Siguiri following a government ban on artisanal mining. The country’s Ministry of Territorial Administration said 13 others were injured during the violence.
Guinea banned artisanal gold mining in Siguiri on November 2, citing environmental damage caused by miners, including pollution of rivers and agricultural land. The clashes erupted on Wednesday as security forces sought to enforce the ban, with protesters reportedly erecting barricades on public roads before gunfire was exchanged.
The ban has also triggered cross-border displacement. Mali said about 100,000 people had arrived in Bamako and nearly 60,000 in the border town of Kouremale after leaving Guinea. Burkina Faso said it had repatriated 45,406 of its citizens who were forced to leave following the restrictions.
Artisanal mining is widespread across West Africa, where rising demand for metals and higher prices have encouraged informal mining activity. The latest violence highlights the difficulties governments face in enforcing mining regulations while managing the livelihoods of communities dependent on the sector.

Explosions and air-raid sirens shook Bahrain around 4:00 a.m. local time on Sunday, 15 November 2026, and a second round followed near 6:30 a.m. Authorities urged residents to take shelter. Bahrain is a small island kingdom in the Gulf that hosts the US Navy’s Fifth Fleet, its main force in the region.
For US readers, a second attack on the island in three days raises questions about American forces, Gulf shipping and the war with Iran.

- Iran’s claim. Iran’s Revolutionary Guards, its elite military force, say they fired six drones at a US radar.
- Result. Bahrain says its air defences intercepted the attacks; no casualties or damage were reported.
- Prediction markets. Bettors on Polymarket, a prediction market, put an effective US-Iran ceasefire by 30 November at 61.5%.

Iran says it targeted a US radar in Bahrain, while Bahrain says its defences stopped the drones. No damage or casualties have been reported.

Explosions were heard around 4:00 a.m. Bahrain time (01:00 GMT) on Sunday, 15 November 2026, and again around 6:30 a.m. Sirens sounded across the kingdom. Bahrain’s Interior Ministry urged residents to stay calm and go to the nearest safe location.
It also asked them to follow official channels for updates. Iran’s Revolutionary Guards, the IRGC (Iran’s elite military force), said they fired six drones at a US air-defence radar system.
They named the Al-Rifaa helicopter base in Bahrain as the target and called it retaliation for “hostile US actions”.Bahrain’s military said its air defences intercepted the attacks before they reached their targets. It blamed Iran’s “systematic hostile approach”.The claim that a US radar was the target comes from Iran.
Nothing we have seen confirms that anything was hit, and no casualties or damage were reported. The attack came two days after a similar one on Friday, 13 November 2026.
The IRGC then claimed it had hit a US early-warning radar in Bahrain.US Central Command (CENTCOM, the American military command for the Middle East) said it shot down two drones that day. It reported no injuries or damage.
Bahrain has therefore been targeted twice in three days. Neither Iranian claim of a radar hit has been confirmed.
Why Bahrain Matters
Bahrain hosts the headquarters of the US Navy’s Fifth Fleet and of Naval Forces Central Command, the navy’s regional command. That makes the island a hub for American naval power in the Gulf.
The war began on 28 February 2026 with US and Israeli strikes on Iran. The United States keeps a naval blockade of Iranian ports.
Shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway between Iran and Oman, has been restricted since the war began. It is a key route for Gulf oil exports.
Peace efforts have not produced a breakthrough, and there is no formal ceasefire. Attacks near a US naval hub therefore matter to anyone who follows the Gulf’s shipping lanes.

What Is Not Known
We do not know whether the radar or any other site was damaged beyond what Bahrain and the United States have said. The total number of drones launched has not been independently confirmed.
It is also unclear whether further attacks will follow. We found no US statement on Sunday’s attack as of publication.

For readers in the United States, the attacks show that the war still reaches Gulf states that host American forces. The reports are journalism, not investment or travel advice.
Anyone planning travel to the region should check the US State Department’s official travel advisories. Bahrain’s Interior Ministry has asked residents to rely on official channels for updates.

The US military's Central Command (CENTCOM) said it had intercepted two Iranian drones during Friday's incident, reporting no casualties or damage. Bahrain's latest interceptions came amid continuing uncertainty over diplomatic efforts to end the conflict.
The war began on February 28 with US and Israeli strikes on Iran and subsequently spread across the region, with Tehran targeting American military installations and infrastructure in Gulf countries. Iran has also restricted shipping through the strategically important Strait of Hormuz.
Bahrain said Iran's continued attacks reflected a systematic hostile approach towards the kingdom. Tehran, meanwhile, warned that any further American aggression would invite a stronger response, reiterating that the Strait of Hormuz remained closed.
Diplomatic efforts to end the nearly nine-month conflict have yet to produce a breakthrough, despite a broader lull in fighting. Iran Launches Six-Drone Assault on U.S. Military Installation in Bahrain as Tehran Threatens Fiercer Retaliation; Strait of Hormuz Crisis Deepens
By: Fern Sidman
Iran launched another drone offensive against an American military installation in Bahrain on Sunday, escalating an increasingly dangerous confrontation with Washington and raising fears that renewed attacks against United States forces could precipitate another devastating military confrontation across the Middle East.
According to a report on Sunday at the BBC, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps announced that it had dispatched six explosive-laden drones toward an American air defense radar installation at the Al-Riffa military base in Bahrain, marking the second attempted attack against the Persian Gulf kingdom within three days.
Bahraini military authorities declared that their air defense systems successfully intercepted the incoming weapons before they could strike their intended targets, contradicting Iranian assertions that the operation had achieved its objectives.
The attack prompted emergency sirens across Bahrain, where the Interior Ministry instructed residents to seek immediate shelter and remain attentive to official security announcements.
The BBC reported that Bahrain’s Foreign Ministry issued a forceful denunciation of Tehran’s actions. “The Kingdom of Bahrain condemns in the strongest terms the continued brutal Iranian attacks on its territory and holds Iran fully responsible for their consequences,” the ministry declared.
The latest confrontation comes as the United States and Iran remain deadlocked over control of the Strait of Hormuz, the strategically indispensable maritime passage through which approximately one-fifth of the world’s petroleum and liquefied natural gas ordinarily travels.
According to the BBC, Iran’s Revolutionary Guards characterized Sunday’s operation as retaliation for American military activities and Washington’s continuing restrictions on Iranian maritime commerce.
In a statement distributed through Iranian state media, the organization warned that the confrontation could intensify. “The Strait of Hormuz is closed, and any aggression by the American enemy will be met with an even harsher and more forceful response,” the Revolutionary Guards declared.
The threat reflects Tehran’s determination to challenge American naval operations protecting commercial vessels traversing the waterway.
Iran maintains that it possesses the authority to restrict maritime passage and has repeatedly threatened vessels it considers unauthorized.
Washington rejects that position and continues providing military protection for oil tankers transporting energy supplies from Gulf Arab countries.
Reuters independently confirmed Sunday’s attack claims, reporting that Iranian forces targeted an American radar installation while Bahraini officials announced successful interceptions. The news agency noted that neither American nor Bahraini authorities had immediately corroborated Iran’s assertion that the radar facility sustained damage.
The BBC reported that the latest assault followed another Iranian drone operation Friday, representing the first attacks against Bahrain since September. During that incident, Iranian officials claimed their forces had struck an American early-warning radar installation.
United States Central Command rejected the assertion, confirming that American forces had intercepted two Iranian drones before either reached its target. Military officials reported no casualties or property damage.
Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty confirmed that Bahrain’s defense forces also intercepted Sunday’s incoming attacks, while the government accused Tehran of continuing a “systematic hostile approach” toward the kingdom. Bahrain’s Foreign Ministry declared that it rejected “turning its territory into an arena for settling scores,” emphasizing that the country should not become a battlefield for Iranian retaliation against Washington.
The repeated attacks are particularly consequential because Bahrain hosts the headquarters of the United States Navy’s Fifth Fleet, a central component of American military operations throughout the Persian Gulf.
The BBC also reported that American forces recently conducted limited military strikes against Iranian installations on Qeshm Island, strategically positioned near the Strait of Hormuz. American officials told CBS News that the operation was defensive and followed Iranian Revolutionary Guard fire directed at an American aircraft. Iranian state media subsequently reported explosions on the island, while the Revolutionary Guards claimed to have destroyed several American unmanned aircraft. Those claims have not been independently verified.
The Washington Post separately confirmed that American strikes had targeted Qeshm Island, quoting an American official who described the operation as “defensive.” The newspaper also reported that repeated Iranian attacks against Bahrain increase the possibility of military miscalculation and further escalation.
The BBC reported that the escalating military confrontation has coincided with the deterioration of diplomatic efforts to resolve the conflict. Washington and Tehran reached a preliminary understanding in June intended to terminate hostilities and restore commercial navigation through the Strait of Hormuz. However, the arrangement subsequently collapsed amid renewed Iranian attacks on shipping and the reimposition of an American naval blockade.
Iranian representatives reportedly proposed reopening the strategic passage within 48 hours if Washington accepted seven conditions, including lifting the blockade and releasing frozen Iranian financial assets. President Donald Trump has nevertheless adopted an increasingly uncompromising position. “We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed,” Trump declared this week.
The president also directed Vice President JD Vance, previously involved in diplomatic efforts, to redirect his attention toward domestic political matters.
ABC News independently reported that negotiations remain stalled despite the earlier diplomatic understanding, while limited exchanges of military strikes continue.
The latest attacks demonstrate how rapidly the confrontation could extend beyond Iran and the United States to neighboring countries hosting American military installations. Bahrain’s geographical proximity to Iran and its longstanding defense relationship with Washington make it particularly vulnerable to retaliatory operations. The Arab League has condemned the attacks and reaffirmed its support for Bahrain’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, according to Al Jazeera.
For global energy markets, the continued disruption of the Strait of Hormuz presents another formidable challenge. Prolonged restrictions on commercial navigation threaten shipping costs, insurance premiums, energy supplies, and the economic stability of countries dependent upon Gulf petroleum exports.
As the BBC’s reporting illustrates, the confrontation now involves overlapping military, diplomatic, and economic pressures that have proved increasingly difficult to contain. Although Bahrain maintains that its defenses successfully prevented Sunday’s attack from achieving its objectives, Iran’s willingness to repeatedly target American military infrastructure underscores the persistent danger of renewed regional warfare.
With diplomatic negotiations stalled and both Washington and Tehran maintaining uncompromising positions, the prospect of another major escalation remains a serious concern for governments throughout the Middle East.

By yourNEWS Media Newsroom
MANAMA, Bahrain — Iran launched drones toward a U.S. military installation in Bahrain on Sunday, Nov. 15, while Saudi-backed forces in Yemen announced their withdrawal from positions overlooking the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, marking two developments in the continuing Middle East conflict.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said it launched six drones targeting an American air defense radar system at the Al-Rifaa helicopter base in Bahrain. Bahraini authorities reported intercepting and destroying the incoming drones before they reached their intended targets.
According to Reuters, the Iranian military described the operation as retaliation for recent American military actions against Iran.
Bahrain’s military confirmed that its air defenses had intercepted several aerial attacks, accusing Tehran of continuing hostile operations against the kingdom.
The attacks triggered warning sirens and emergency alerts directing residents to seek shelter. No injuries or damage were immediately reported from the intercepted drones.
Bahrain hosts the headquarters of the U.S. Navy’s Fifth Fleet and serves as a major operational center for American naval forces in the Persian Gulf.
Sunday’s attack followed another attempted Iranian drone strike against an American radar facility in Bahrain on Friday. U.S. Central Command reported intercepting two drones during that incident without casualties or damage.
Bahrain’s Foreign Ministry condemned the renewed attacks, describing them as a violation of international law and rejecting Iran’s justification for targeting facilities on Bahraini territory.
Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Jordan and Egypt also condemned the attacks and expressed support for Bahrain.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said Tehran would continue responding to military actions by the United States and other countries. Asked whether the latest attacks indicated a change in Iran’s position during stalled negotiations, Baghaei said the country was focused on protecting its security.
The developments occurred as Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces announced their withdrawal from positions near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a narrow waterway connecting the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden.
The withdrawal followed a six-week offensive aimed at removing Houthi fighters from territory overlooking the strategic shipping passage.
In a statement reported by The Guardian, the Southern Armed Forces, a principal military organization supporting Yemen’s internationally recognized government, announced that troops were being redeployed from Dhubab Airport and the Bab el-Mandeb area.
The force said the redeployment was intended to strengthen defenses around Aden, the temporary seat of Yemen’s internationally recognized government, and neighboring governorates.
Yemeni military sources said the withdrawing troops had moved toward al-Suqyah, approximately 150 kilometers west of Aden.
The retreat followed territorial advances by the Houthis during September, when the Iran-aligned movement captured substantial portions of Yemen’s Red Sea coastline and expanded its presence near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
Government forces subsequently regained some positions during an October counteroffensive but failed to dislodge the Houthis from several coastal areas, including the port city of al-Mocha.
The Bab el-Mandeb Strait is a major passage for commercial shipping and energy exports traveling between the Indian Ocean, Red Sea and Suez Canal. Control of adjacent coastal territory can affect the security of vessels using the route.
The Houthis have continued launching missiles and drones toward Saudi Arabia and targets associated with the Yemeni government.
The Saudi-led coalition reported Sunday that it had intercepted two Houthi ballistic missiles directed toward Riyadh and three drones over Saudi Arabia’s Eastern Province.
Separately, Yemeni government and military sources reported that a Houthi missile attack near Aden killed five people and wounded eight others.
The Associated Press reported that government-aligned forces had withdrawn from positions near the strait, allowing the Houthis to strengthen their presence in the area.
The fighting has also disrupted humanitarian operations. United Nations officials have warned that insecurity near Lahj has complicated assistance for thousands of African refugees.
Meanwhile, Iran’s Revolutionary Guard claimed that naval mines had struck commercial tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, causing explosions and fires. Those claims had not been independently verified.
The Strait of Hormuz remains another major concern for international shipping because of its importance to global oil and natural gas exports.
The latest developments come as negotiations between Washington and Tehran remain stalled following months of military operations that began with U.S. and Israeli strikes against Iran in February.
President Donald Trump has reportedly told senior advisers that he may refrain from launching additional major attacks against Iran unless Tehran or its regional allies undertake further actions against American interests.
The administration has maintained military forces in the region while continuing economic restrictions and naval operations affecting Iranian commerce.
Iranian officials have said they will respond to additional attacks, while regional governments have encouraged diplomatic efforts to prevent further escalation.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi is expected to visit Oman, which has previously served as an intermediary in negotiations involving Tehran and Washington.
As of Sunday, Bahraini authorities reported that their defenses had prevented the Iranian drones from reaching their targets, while Saudi-backed Yemeni forces continued repositioning around Aden following their withdrawal from the Bab el-Mandeb area.
The separate developments leave American military facilities in the Gulf and commercial shipping routes near Yemen facing continued security threats as diplomatic efforts remain unresolved.

sources.news_title: Bahrain says air defenses intercepted Iranian aerial attacks before reaching targets
Iran Fires Drones at Bahrain as Trump Weighs Strike Pause
sources.text:
A vessel leaving the Strait of Hormuz was struck by an unidentified projectile on Monday morning, starting an engine-room fire with no casualties reported, the British maritime agency UKMTO said, a day after Iran's Revolutionary Guard said it launched six drones at a U.S. air defense radar at Riffa Air Base in Bahrain. It was the Guard's second claimed attack on a U.S. radar there in three days, and the Bahrain Defense Force said its air defenses thwarted several Iranian aerial attacks before the drones reached their targets. The Bahrain claim could not be independently verified, and the U.S. military had not commented on it publicly. The Gulf Cooperation Council's secretary general, Jasem Al Budaiwi, called the attack a blatant challenge to regional peace efforts, and Qatar, the main mediator between Washington and Tehran, called it a dangerous escalation that could undermine diplomacy. Bahrain's Foreign Ministry said the kingdom rejects turning its territory into an arena for settling scores and holds Iran fully responsible for the attacks and their consequences. Saudi Arabia, Jordan and Egypt also condemned them, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio condemned the attacks in a call Monday with Bahraini Foreign Minister Abdullatif al-Zayani. It came a day after a report, citing three people familiar with the discussions, said President Donald Trump has told senior advisers he may hold off on attacking Iran if neither Tehran nor the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen provoke the United States again. A White House official said Trump is the sole decision-maker and that only he knows what he will do and when.
Iran said Saturday that three more oil tankers had struck mines in the Strait of Hormuz overnight, and its Revolutionary Guard claimed it shot down another U.S. drone, as the diplomatic track that President Donald Trump called unnecessary on Thursday showed no sign of restarting. The Guard said two tankers, one of them a supertanker, had switched off their radar and positioning systems while using an unauthorized route in the southern part of the strait. Iran's navy said a third tanker caught fire and stopped after hitting a mine in a prohibited zone east of the waterway. Iran did not name the ships or their owners, and none of the reports could be independently verified. The Guard also said a new air defense system downed an American MQ-1 Predator over Qeshm Island, on the strait's northern coast, and Iranian officials described it as the second Predator lost in two days and the 17th of the war. The U.S. military did not immediately comment.
President Donald Trump said Thursday that the United States no longer needs an agreement with Iran and directed Vice President JD Vance, who had led Washington's diplomacy with Tehran, to turn his full attention to alleged corruption in Democratic-run states and cities. The announcement came a day after reports that Vance was weighing a face-to-face meeting with Iran's security chief, and it appeared to close, at least for now, the most visible diplomatic track of a war now in its ninth month.
"We don't need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed," Trump wrote on his social media platform shortly after 8 a.m. Eastern. "We've got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we've got their Strait!" In the same post he said he had asked Vance to focus his "complete and total attention" on what he called massive corruption and crime in Democrat-run cities and states, alleging that billions of dollars are being stolen every month.
The post suggested that Trump is dialing back diplomatic efforts and ending Vance's negotiating role in favor of leaving the naval blockade of Iranian ports in place and continuing to squeeze Iran's economy. The White House did not go that far in public. An administration official declined to say whether talks with Iran have stopped, saying instead that the blockade, which the White House calls Operation Economic Outcast, and the newer Operation Iron Gate would continue with full effect and that Trump would make sure Iran never obtains a nuclear weapon. Trump's statement did not mention the military options he has discussed in recent weeks, and it did not say who, if anyone, now speaks for the United States in contacts with Tehran.
Hours later, Trump went further in describing what he wants from the war. Asked in a radio interview whether it would be a defeat if Iran's current rulers are still in power when he leaves office, he answered: "Yes, that would be a defeat. Yeah, I would say that would be a defeat. Absolutely." He said the Iranian government was collapsing. Asked whether he would hesitate to use military force to stop Iran from threatening American allies and ships, he said, "No hesitation," and added, "If I saw things going the other way, I would do that, and it's possible I would do it right now."
The remarks set a higher bar than the administration has usually described. Officials have generally framed the war's aims in terms of Iran's nuclear program, its missiles and the Strait of Hormuz, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio said this week that economic pressure was achieving the objectives of military action. A president who says the survival of Iran's leadership would count as a defeat is describing an outcome that neither a blockade nor a negotiated settlement is designed to guarantee. Trump also issued a warning over threats against American officials. Asked what would happen if Iran killed a U.S. official such as Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, he said, "They will not exist any longer."
In interviews that aired Thursday evening, Trump also said "we haven't lost a soldier in five months, and we control the Gulf," a claim about American casualties that news reports have described as false. In a separate interview, he said he could end the war swiftly but has not because neighboring Gulf countries, which he called "tremendous investors" in the United States, have asked him not to escalate. Asked about a request by Gulf states for a waiting period before any new attacks, he said he was not sure he agreed.
Vance had become the central American figure in those contacts. Trump assigned him to lead negotiations earlier this year, and Iranian state media said late last month that Tehran had received a letter from the vice president seeking renewed talks. On Wednesday, U.S. and Middle Eastern officials cited in news reports said Vance was considering direct talks with Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, possibly in Doha, and that Trump had told aides he was open to Vance restarting negotiations. No meeting had been scheduled. A person familiar with the matter said Trump knew of those deliberations before he posted and believed the Iranians were not acting in good faith. Rezaei, asked about meeting Vance, said, "Absolutely not."
The reassignment follows an unusually public difference between the president and his vice president. After Republicans lost control of Congress in the Nov. 3 midterm elections, Vance wrote that the war with Iran was the main reason for the defeat. Trump said last weekend that the comments had not affected their relationship but that many conservatives did not like them, and he has defended the war as necessary to stop Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon. Former Vice President Mike Pence disputed Vance's assessment this week, saying Americans grew frustrated not because Trump launched the war but because his administration had not finished it, and he blamed an "air of corruption" and self-dealing in Trump's second term for the party's losses. Officials have also said that Trump privately questioned whether the memorandum of understanding he signed with Iran's president in June, which Vance helped negotiate, was a costly mistake that gave Tehran time to regroup and earn oil revenue before the blockade began. Other White House officials have denied that account.
The decision aligns Trump with the advisers who have argued for pressure over negotiation. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Tuesday in Paris that there is no need for major combat operations because the economic campaign is achieving the same objectives, and he called Iran's demands, including reparations for the war, absurd. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and CIA Director John Ratcliffe have favored the same course. A report Saturday, citing U.S. officials, said intelligence agencies assess the blockade and sanctions are hurting Iran's economy and that renewed strikes would do little to change Tehran's negotiating demands. It also reported that Trump told Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman on Oct. 31 that he planned to attack after the elections and that the crown prince asked him to hold off, arguing that sanctions were working, according to two people familiar with the conversation. Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has also urged restraint, and neither leader won a commitment. Trump said Monday that Iran is militarily "effectively over," and at a Veterans Day ceremony on Wednesday he said U.S. forces had already beaten Iran but that he wants a "total victory."
Trump's two claims in Thursday's post describe the leverage he believes he holds. The money is a reference to Iranian assets frozen abroad and to revenue lost under sanctions and the blockade. The strait is the Strait of Hormuz, where U.S. forces have been working to secure passage for shipping. Commercial traffic through the waterway remains a fraction of what it was before the war, and Iran says it will stay closed until Washington meets its conditions. Tehran's forces continue to report incidents involving tankers there almost daily, which is difficult to square with the claim that the United States controls it.
Iran answered in kind. President Masoud Pezeshkian said Thursday that the United States was gradually being brought to its knees as Iran resisted pressure, according to Iranian media. A senior spokesman for Iran's armed forces, Brig. Gen. Abolfazl Shekarchi, warned that the response to any new American attack would be "10 times" more severe, after Trump said a future U.S. strike would be five times stronger than previous ones. Rezaei said Iran would not send "a single atom" of its enriched nuclear stockpile abroad, and Iranian officials repeated that Washington must accept Tehran's seven conditions. Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, a senior negotiator, said Sunday that the path to ending the conflict remains open if Washington accepts Iran's "logical conditions," that Tehran will not stay in a state of "neither war nor peace," and that its armed forces will "determine the geography of battle" if the United States resumes strikes, according to Iranian media.
The exchange of threats turned into action on Friday. Iran's Revolutionary Guard said its aerospace force had targeted and destroyed a U.S. early-warning radar on Bahrain, which hosts the headquarters of the U.S. Navy's Fifth Fleet, and described the strike as retaliation for what it called an air attack on a telecommunications tower in Sirik, a coastal town in southern Iran east of the Strait of Hormuz. Iranian state media said Sirik was hit on Thursday but did not say by whom. U.S. Central Command rejected the claim, saying the Guard had launched two one-way attack drones toward Bahrain, that U.S. forces shot down both and that there was no damage or injury. The Guard said it was on full alert to respond "without limits" if the United States repeats what it called acts of aggression. Rezaei, in an interview with a Lebanese television channel broadcast Wednesday, had said Iran would strike American bases in Europe and other distant locations if aircraft used them to attack Iran. Neither account of Friday's incident could be independently verified. The Guard returned to Bahrain on Sunday, when sirens sounded twice across the kingdom, the first at about 4:30 a.m. local time, and the Interior Ministry told residents to stay calm and go to the nearest safe location.
An Israeli television report said Trump's statement followed a message from Iran to Qatar, the main mediator, that it had no intention of negotiating over its nuclear program. That report has not been confirmed. Iran has refused to discuss its nuclear program until Washington accepts its ceasefire conditions, a position consistent with that report. Iran has not published its full list of conditions, but officials have said they include lifting sanctions and the blockade and ending the fighting on all fronts, and Tehran has said the strait could reopen within two days if they are met.
Iran's Assembly of Experts, the clerical body responsible for choosing and overseeing the supreme leader, added a nuclear dimension on Thursday. In a statement reported by state television, it said that examining withdrawal from the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons, revising the country's defense doctrine and building the necessary deterrence had become an "unavoidable necessity" and a public and national demand, citing repeated threats against the country. The statement calls for examining the step rather than announcing it, and Iranian officials have argued over treaty membership for months without a decision. Leaving the treaty would remove Iran from the treaty's safeguards and inspection system, a step that would run directly against the aim Trump has cited for the war. Iran also told the International Atomic Energy Agency this month, in a confidential report sent to member states, that discussions on nuclear monitoring cannot proceed while it is under threat of military attack, citing what it called persistent, explicit and public threats by Trump. The agency has called on Iran to restore access to its nuclear sites. Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said in a televised interview late Sunday that Iran will not grant the agency access to damaged facilities until the war has permanently ended, and he said the request was likely aimed at assessing the effectiveness of American weaponry.
At sea, the pattern of the past week continued. Iran's navy said four oil tankers were hit by explosions in the strait over Wednesday and Thursday, including two that caught fire Thursday after striking mines in the eastern part of the strait, and on Friday it said a tanker carrying liquefied natural gas struck a mine on what it called an unauthorized and dangerous route. It reported three more on Saturday. It said the ships had entered a restricted area despite warnings and with their radar switched off, and it placed responsibility on the U.S. president and on the vessels' owners. On Sunday, the Guard's naval forces claimed that one oil tanker sank and a second was damaged after striking mines, saying both had switched off their tracking systems. On Monday morning, UKMTO said a vessel on an outbound transit of the strait was struck by an unknown projectile, and Iran's state broadcaster said, citing the navy, that a tanker east of the strait caught fire after hitting a mine; it was not clear whether the two reports described the same ship. The claims could not be independently verified. Iranian forces made similar announcements about three tankers on Tuesday and three the previous Sunday. Separately, UKMTO said a Liberia-flagged crude tanker, the Dominica Prosperity, was struck by an unidentified projectile on Wednesday evening about 14 nautical miles northwest of Ras al-Khaimah in the United Arab Emirates, setting its engine-room area on fire. All 22 crew members, 19 of them Indian nationals, were evacuated without injuries, according to India's shipping minister, and no party has been named as responsible.
Tehran has also warned South Korea against moving closer to the strait. After South Korea's Cabinet approved expanding the operating area of its Cheonghae naval unit to waters south of Oman, about 400 miles from the strait, Iran's foreign ministry spokesman urged Seoul to refrain from deploying military forces, and an Iranian post on social media on Thursday quoted a Korean proverb in a sharper warning. Seoul says the unit will not join the war.
The conflict also widened on the Arabian Peninsula. Yemen's Houthi movement, which is aligned with Iran, said Thursday that it had attacked a pumping station on Saudi Arabia's East-West oil pipeline and an oil facility in the Red Sea city of Yanbu, and it also claimed strikes on a Saudi Aramco facility in Riyadh and an air base at Khamis Mushait. Saudi authorities had not commented on those claims. A day earlier, the Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted three cruise missiles heading toward Riyadh and two drones and two ballistic missiles over western Saudi Arabia. Houthi authorities say Saudi strikes on Sanaa province over the weekend killed 44 people, including more than 20 children, a toll that could not be independently verified. On Sunday, Yemen's Southern Armed Forces, the main force fighting for the internationally recognized government in the south, announced they were withdrawing from Dhubab Airport and the Bab al-Mandeb area to defend Aden, signaling the apparent end of a six-week Saudi-backed counteroffensive. The Saudi-led coalition said the same day that it shot down two drones launched over the Mecca region; the Houthis have not commented on that alleged attack.
The targets matter because of what the pipeline is for. The East-West line carries crude from Saudi Arabia's eastern oil fields to Yanbu on the Red Sea, allowing exports to bypass the Strait of Hormuz. It has been the kingdom's main alternative route since the strait was closed to most traffic. Attacks on it, if confirmed, would threaten the workaround that has kept part of the Gulf's oil reaching world markets.
Oil prices reversed course after Trump's post on Thursday. Brent crude, which had been falling earlier in the day on signs of higher Saudi exports, climbed as much as 1.8 percent to top $94 a barrel, and U.S. crude rose above $87. On Friday, prices were mixed and edged higher by midday in Europe, with Brent up about 0.9 percent at $96.67 a barrel and U.S. crude up 0.5 percent at $89.18, but both benchmarks were on course for a second straight weekly decline of about 2 percent, after falls of 16 percent for Brent and 13 percent for U.S. crude the week before. Analysts attributed the weakness to expectations that Washington will rely on the blockade and sanctions rather than major combat, and to rising U.S. crude and fuel inventories. Brent had dropped below $90 on Tuesday for the first time since late August. The swing shows how closely the market follows statements from Washington while the strait remains largely shut.
The case for waiting rests on Iran's economy. A U.S. Treasury assessment prepared for Trump says no new oil has been loaded onto tankers at Iran's export terminals since late August and that annual inflation approached 90 percent in September, describing the economy as crippled without concluding that it is near collapse. U.S. Central Command says its blockade had redirected 144 commercial vessels through the end of October. The strategy assumes that Iran's economy will deteriorate faster than Washington's tolerance for the war's costs.
Those costs are not only Iran's. The closure of the strait and the attacks on Gulf energy sites have kept fuel prices high, and U.S. consumer prices rose more than expected in October, a report that has strengthened expectations of another Federal Reserve rate increase next month. A policy of indefinite blockade without negotiations would extend the period in which energy markets, shipping insurers and Gulf governments operate under wartime conditions.
Israel, which fought alongside the United States when the war began on Feb. 28, signaled continuity. Its defense chief said Thursday that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and the military are united on Iran policy and that all decisions are made in full cooperation between the political and military leadership, though an Israeli television report this week said military chief of staff Eyal Zamir had again opposed unspecified steps that Netanyahu wants to take. Mossad Director Roman Gofman visited Washington this week, met CIA Director John Ratcliffe and pressed for a resumption of the war, according to a report that has not been confirmed. Israel's own politics are in transition after the Oct. 27 election, in which Netanyahu's bloc won 53 seats to 48 for the alliance led by Gadi Eisenkot, who now holds the mandate to form the next government.
In Washington, the announcement lands in the middle of a fight over the war's conduct. Democrats take control of both chambers of Congress in January and have said they will investigate the war, press for a vote on war powers and pursue Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who survived an impeachment effort in the House this week. A fight over money comes first. Four Democratic senators, Michael Bennet, Bernie Sanders, Chris Van Hollen and Tammy Duckworth, said Thursday they would oppose a short-term funding bill that does not restrict war spending, and top Democrats have demanded that Iran war funding be left out of any deal to avert a shutdown when government funding expires on Dec. 11. A president who says no deal is needed will face a Congress that campaigned in part on ending the conflict. In a separate interview on Thursday, Trump said he was disappointed in people who voted against Republicans over the war, calling the higher costs a very small price to pay to stop a country he said would use nuclear weapons. "I don't think it was the war as much as what the war did," he said of the election result.
The task Trump gave Vance is tied to that fight as well. Corruption was among the issues that broke in Democrats' favor in the election, and Democrats have promised investigations of the president's family finances and of his administration. Trump has responded by accusing Democrats of corruption and of illegally threatening Republicans, and his White House counsel has warned that their planned inquiries could amount to crimes. Putting the vice president in charge of a campaign against alleged corruption in Democratic-run jurisdictions turns the administration's most senior war skeptic toward a domestic political battle.
The military posture is growing rather than easing. Thousands of U.S. troops remain in the waters off Iran enforcing the blockade, and the aircraft carrier USS Theodore Roosevelt entered the Central Command area on Sunday, a U.S. official said, putting three U.S. carrier strike groups in the region. The Roosevelt was originally due to relieve the USS George Washington, which has stayed in the region for now, and Central Command said Monday that the Roosevelt was operating in its area. Officials have said Central Command has completed preparations that would allow a return to major combat operations if ordered. Iran has said its forces will not wait for a confirmed hostile act before responding, and its Revolutionary Guard said last week that it had lifted a self-imposed limit on the range of its ballistic missiles. The Guard also said Monday that its drone unit used electronic warfare to take control of a U.S. MQM-170 drone; the claim could not be independently verified.
The risks have reached senior American officials personally. Bessent, the architect of the economic campaign, has moved from his Washington home to a military base amid Iranian threats against him, a move the Treasury Department confirmed this week, and he has said the threats will not force him to live in fear. The Justice Department this week charged three men it described as Iranian-backed operatives over plots in the United States and Europe, including one against a British air base used by American bombers.
There are at least three ways to read Thursday's statement. One is as a negotiating tactic, meant to convince Tehran that Washington is prepared to walk away and that its conditions will not be met. A second is as a real change of policy toward an open-ended blockade in which no agreement is sought and the war ends only when Iran's position collapses. A third is as a matter of internal politics, in which the president has sidelined a vice president who publicly blamed the war for the party's losses. The three are not mutually exclusive, and the White House's refusal to say whether talks have ended leaves each of them open. His later remark that the survival of Iran's rulers would be a defeat lends weight to the second reading, though he did not say how that outcome would be achieved. Saturday's report adds a condition to that reading: a hold-off that depends on Iran and the Houthis avoiding new provocations is hard to square with the Guard's claimed attacks on a U.S. radar in Bahrain on Friday and Sunday and the Houthis' claimed strikes on Saudi oil facilities.
The mediators have not said where this leaves them. Qatar's prime minister met Trump and Vance at the White House on Monday and described the meetings as excellent, and Doha has said it has received positive responses from both sides while acknowledging uncertainty about the prospects for a deal. Qatar's emir and Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan have also signed a mutual defense agreement in Istanbul. European governments and the Group of Seven have called for a diplomatic effort to end the conflict and reopen the strait. Trump has said Gulf countries have asked him not to escalate, though he said he was not sure he agreed with their request for a waiting period.
Vance's reassignment removes the senior official most visibly tied to the Qatari channel, and neither the White House nor Tehran has said whether that channel stays open. The 60-day negotiating window opened by the initial June agreement has lapsed without a deal. Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said Monday at a meeting of the Economic Cooperation Organization that a 10-nation regional bloc had backed Tehran's proposal to reopen the strait under an initial ceasefire with the United States, a plan the Trump administration has so far rejected; the bloc's backing could not be independently confirmed. Araghchi is due in Muscat on Tuesday to meet Omani Foreign Minister Badr al-Busaidi, Iran's Foreign Ministry said, and an Iranian lawmaker, Hassan Ghashghavi, said Monday that Iran and Oman had nearly finished a joint plan governing navigation through the strait, while Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said the two sides had reached a mutual understanding on a shipping corridor and traffic separation scheme. The terms of that plan have not been published. The Houthis have said they are preparing to advance on Aden after the government's pullback at Bab al-Mandeb, and Iran's Assembly of Experts has called for examining a withdrawal from the Non-Proliferation Treaty. Trump left Washington on Monday for Manila and then travels to the APEC summit in Shenzhen, where a three-way meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin is set for Thursday. U.S. officials say he intends to raise Iran and nuclear arms reductions there and does not expect to discuss Ukraine. Oil markets jumped on Thursday's post and then eased, pricing a blockade that holds without a return to major combat.
The president has said in plain terms that he sees no need to negotiate and that he will count it a defeat if Iran's rulers are still in place when he leaves office, while telling advisers, according to a report, that he may hold off on new strikes if there are no new provocations. Iran has said in equally plain terms that it will not yield, its Guard has now claimed two attacks on a U.S. radar in Bahrain within three days, and a ship was struck leaving the strait on Monday morning. The blockade continues, the strait is still largely closed, and the official who was trying to arrange a meeting between the two sides has been given a different job.

sources.news_title: Iran launches drone strike on U.S. base in Bahrain
Iran launches second attack in three days on Bahrain; drones shot down before hitting targets
Irans Guards say attacked military base in Bahrain with drones
sources.text:
Iran's Revolutionary Guards said their forces carried out a drone attack on a US radar system at a base in Bahrain, according to a statement carried by the Iranian state broadcaster on Sunday.
"The U.S. air defense radar system at the Al-Riffa helicopter base in Bahrain was targeted by six drones belonging to the IRGC Aerospace Force," the Guards said in a statement posted by the state broadcaster on Telegram.
Blasts and sirens rang out over Bahrain and authorities urged residents to seek shelter on Sunday as Iran's Guards said they had attacked a US military base in the Gulf nation.
Alarm sirens blared, according to an AFP journalist, while authorities posted several alerts on social media, without specifying the source of the threat.
The interior ministry in an X post urged "residents to remain calm, proceed to the nearest safe location, and follow news through official channels for the protection of public safety".
Explosions could be heard around 4:00 am (0100 GMT), the AFP journalist said, with residents reporting a second series of blasts around 6:30 am (0330 GMT).
In a statement carried by state-run broadcaster IRIB, the IRGC said the Strait of Hormuz remains closed, mentioning what it called Washington's "failure" to escort ships through the waterway.
It warned that "any US aggression would be met with an even harsher and more devastating response."
The developments come amid continued tensions between Iran and the US over navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, a strategic waterway for global energy and commodity supplies.
Navigation through the strait has also been a key issue in negotiations between Washington and Tehran.
The war began with US and Israeli attacks on Iran on Feb. 28, before the sides reached a ceasefire in April.
Fighting between Washington and Tehran later resumed as negotiations stalled, despite the two sides signing a memorandum of understanding in June.

sources.news_title: Iran launches second drone attack on Bahrain in just three days
sources.text:
Iran sent drones toward Bahrain on Sunday for the second time in three days, with Bahraini authorities saying their defenses destroyed the incoming threats before they reached their targets.
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said six drones were deployed against an American air-defense radar installation at Bahrain’s al-Riffa air base. Bahrain, which hosts the US Fifth Fleet, issued an alert instructing residents to seek shelter.
Bahrain’s Foreign Ministry condemned the attacks and said Tehran would bear responsibility for their consequences.
The incident followed Friday’s attempted strike, which the IRGC claimed had hit an American early-warning radar facility. The US military rejected that account, saying its forces downed both Iranian attack drones and that nobody was hurt and no damage occurred.
Saudi Arabia’s Defense Ministry also announced Sunday that its air defenses had shot down two drones launched by the Houthis from Yemen after they entered airspace over the Mecca region in western Saudi Arabia. The ministry did not immediately identify their intended targets or report whether the attack caused damage.
The announcement followed several days of reported interceptions. Saudi authorities said they destroyed Houthi drones over the Mecca and southern regions on November 11, and intercepted two more heading toward the Riyadh and southern regions on November 14.
Reuters reported on November 12 that debris from two intercepted ballistic missiles fell at two locations in the Mecca region. The Houthis have repeatedly denied targeting the cities of Mecca and Medina, saying their attacks are directed at military and strategic facilities.
In a statement carried by Iranian state media on Sunday, the IRGC declared, “The Strait of Hormuz is closed," and threatened a stronger response to American military action.
Washington and Tehran remain at odds over access to the waterway. Iran has targeted vessels it considers to be operating without its authorization, while American forces have been protecting oil tankers carrying Gulf exports.
The IRGC also claimed Sunday that naval mines had struck two tankers in the strait, leaving them burning. Reuters said it could not independently confirm the claim.
Earlier in the week, American forces struck Qeshm Island after the IRGC fired at a US aircraft, US officials told CBS. The officials characterized the operation as defensive and limited in scope.
A preliminary June arrangement intended to end the conflict and restore passage through Hormuz unraveled after renewed Iranian attacks on shipping and the reinstatement of Washington’s blockade of Iranian ports.
President Donald Trump said this week that he was no longer pursuing an agreement with Tehran and directed Vice President JD Vance to concentrate on domestic politics. Reuters reported Saturday that Trump had indicated he could refrain from further strikes if Iran and the Houthis avoided new provocations, while keeping the blockade in place.
Meanwhile, Saudi-backed troops fighting the Iran-aligned Houthis in Yemen announced Sunday that they were leaving positions near Bab el-Mandeb and Dhubab Airport to strengthen defenses around Aden, the internationally recognized government’s temporary capital.
The Southern Armed Forces said the redeployment prioritized protecting Aden and surrounding governorates. Neither Saudi Arabia nor the Houthis immediately commented on the withdrawal.
According to Reuters, the retreat appeared to bring a six-week counteroffensive to a close. Government troops had recovered several positions near the strait but had been unable to fully dislodge the Houthis or recapture Mocha.
Yemeni military sources told Reuters that withdrawing units had moved to al-Suqyah, roughly 150 kilometers west of Aden, while continuing operations against nearby Houthi coastal positions.
Conditions have also deteriorated in besieged Taiz, where approximately half of the 300,000 people displaced by the latest fighting are sheltering. Relief supplies cannot reach the city, and civilians are unable to leave.
Iranian state media reported that Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi would travel to Oman on Tuesday for discussions with his counterpart. Oman has served as a mediator in the crisis.

sources.news_title: Iran launches drone attack on US base in Bahrain
sources.text:
Iran launches drone attack on US base in Bahrain
Iran has carried out another drone attack targeting a US military installation in Bahrain, marking its second attempt to strike the Gulf country in three days.
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, IRGC, said it deployed six drones against a US air defence radar facility at Al-Riffa air base on Sunday.
However, Bahrain's military said its air defence systems intercepted and destroyed the drones before they could reach their targets.
The latest attack follows another Iranian drone assault on Bahrain on Friday, which was the country's first strike against Gulf states since September.
The attacks come amid growing tensions between Iran and the United States over control of the Strait of Hormuz, a major shipping route through which about 20 per cent of the world's oil and gas supplies normally pass.
Commercial shipping through the strait has been heavily disrupted since the war began in February.
Iran insists that it has the right to control the waterway and has targeted vessels it describes as unauthorised. Meanwhile, the US military has been escorting oil tankers to protect shipments from Gulf Arab countries.
As air raid sirens sounded across Bahrain on Sunday, the country's Interior Ministry urged residents to move to the nearest safe locations.
Bahrain's Foreign Ministry condemned the attack, saying: "The Kingdom of Bahrain condemns in the strongest terms the continued brutal Iranian attacks on its territory and holds Iran fully responsible for their consequences."
In a statement broadcast by Iran's state media on Telegram, the IRGC warned that further American aggression would attract a stronger response.
"The Strait of Hormuz is closed, and any aggression by the American enemy will be met with an even harsher and more forceful response," the statement said.
Earlier, the IRGC claimed it had struck a US early-warning radar system in Bahrain during Friday's attack.
However, the US military rejected the claim, saying two Iranian one-way attack drones were launched towards Bahrain but were intercepted by American forces. It added that no one was injured and no damage was recorded.
The latest confrontation follows US strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz earlier in the week.

sources.news_title: Sirens send Bahrain residents to shelters as drones target US radar base
sources.text:
Sirens send Bahrain residents to shelters as drones target U.S. radar base
(TNND) — Air-raid sirens sent residents scrambling for shelter in Bahrain early Sunday as the kingdom said it intercepted six Iranian drones aimed at a U.S. air-defense radar facility at Al-Rifaa air base, the latest escalation in a fast-moving confrontation tied to the war and mounting U.S.-Iran tensions.
Bahrain said the drones were stopped before reaching their targets. Iran, however, claimed it struck a base. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said the attack was in retaliation for “hostile US actions.”
Bahrain’s Interior Ministry urged residents to go to their nearest safe location as the sirens sounded.
Sunday’s incident marked Iran’s second attempt to target Bahrain in three days and the first such attacks since a wave of strikes in September.
On Friday, Iran said it had hit a U.S. early-warning radar facility in Bahrain. U.S. Central Command said two drones were shot down, with no injuries or damage.
Bahrain hosts key U.S. military facilities, including the U.S. Navy’s Fifth Fleet and Naval Forces Central Command headquarters.
The strikes come as the U.S. maintains a naval blockade of Iranian ports and both countries contest control of the Strait of Hormuz. Roughly one-fifth of the world’s oil and gas supply typically passes through the strait, where shipping has been restricted since the war began in February.
The U.S. has carried out limited strikes on Iranian targets, including sites on Qeshm Island. Iran has said it will keep responding to what it calls military aggression.
Peace efforts remain stalled. President Donald Trump has described the war as “effectively over,” while the Guardian reported he said Washington was no longer seeking a deal.
Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Jordan, and Egypt condemned the attacks and expressed solidarity with Bahrain.

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps claimed it launched six drones at a U.S. air-defense radar at the Al-Riffa helicopter base, which hosts American forces. That claimed hit has not been confirmed by Bahrain or the United States.

The Bahrain Defence Force announced that its units remained at the highest level of readiness after confronting the incoming attack.

The US and Iran are locked in a stand-off over the Strait of Hormuz. About a fifth of the world's gas and oil supply usually flows through it but shipping has been restricted since the outbreak of war in February.

In a statement on the strikes shared by Iran's state broadcaster on Telegram, the IRGC said: "The Strait of Hormuz is closed, and any aggression by the American enemy will be met with an even harsher and more forceful response."
