Iran and its allies ramped up pressure on the U.S. and allied Gulf states on two fronts on Sunday, with Saudi-backed forces retreating in their battle against the Iran-aligned Houthis in Yemen and Iran itself firing drones at U.S. bases in Bahrain.
In Yemen, Saudi Arabia's campaign against the Houthis suffered a major setback, as its allies, fighting on behalf of the internationally recognized Yemeni government, pulled back from the Bab el-Mandeb Strait to defend their temporary capital Aden on the southern coast.
The announcement signaled the apparent end of a six-week government counteroffensive to drive the Houthis from the mouth of the Red Sea to secure a key oil route.
Meanwhile, Iranian attacks on Bahrain, headquarters of the U.S. Fifth Fleet in the Gulf, were likely to put new pressure on U.S. President Donald Trump to resolve the war he launched nearly nine months ago.
Since the unpopular war contributed to a defeat for his Republicans in midterm elections this month, Trump has played down the need for a diplomatic breakthrough.
Major warfare between the U.S. and Iran has calmed since the early phase of the conflict, but with diplomacy stalled there is little immediate prospect of a resolution either to the wider conflict or the war in Yemen.
Houthi gains
Sunday's announcement of a Yemeni government retreat raises the prospect of new Houthi advances towards Aden on the southern coast, base of the internationally recognized government since the Houthis drove it from the capital Sanaa more than a decade ago.
"The Southern Armed Forces announce the implementation of a redeployment operation for its forces from Dhubab Airport and the Bab el-Mandeb area, west of Taiz Governorate," the main military force fighting for Yemen's government in the south of the country said in a statement.
"This step is taken based on the priority of securing the capital, Aden, and the neighboring governorates, as well as strengthening the front lines and addressing existing threats."
There was no immediate response from the Houthis or from Saudi Arabia.
The retreat signals a setback for efforts to reverse rapid gains the Houthis made in September to capture the coast along the Red Sea and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait that controls access to it.
A Saudi-backed government offensive last month retook key positions around the strait but failed to drive the Houthis entirely away from the area or retake the city of al-Mocha further up the coast.
The Houthis have responded by intensifying drone and missile attacks on Saudi Arabia, grounding flights with strikes on its main airports as well as setting global oil markets on edge by targeting energy facilities.
On Sunday, the militant group said it attacked the King Khalid International Airport and a financial center in Riyadh and two pumping stations on the East-West oil pipeline.
There was no immediate Saudi confirmation.
With the conflict in the Middle East disrupting oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz, Riyadh has rerouted about 4 million barrels per day of crude via the East-West Pipeline to Yanbu, equivalent to about 4% of global supply.
Yemeni military sources said government forces around the Bab el-Mandeb had redeployed to al-Suqyah, 150 km (95 miles) west of Aden, though they were still trying to push the Houthis from nearby coastal areas.
In the highlands north of Aden, where the Houthis have besieged Yemen's third-largest city, Taiz, the fighters are now positioned just outside the district of Tur al-Bahah, about 80 km (50 miles) from the city, the sources said.
Humanitarian conditions are worsening in Taiz, which hosts about half of the 300,000 people displaced across Yemen by the latest fighting. Aid supplies cannot enter, and civilians cannot leave.

Fresh Iranian strikes on Bahrain, home to U.S. bases, could undermine Trump's desire to turn the page on the war following his Republicans' midterm election rout.

The complaint also claims the post — known as Port Shuaiba — "had no physician, no fixed aid station, and only one ambulance."
"I feel this is a tactical failure by the Army, our leadership, and myself - all the way down to my level," Maj. Ramsbottom told 60 Minutes. "We just did not plan this well, and this needs to be a lesson that we learn."
Ramsbottom spoke with 60 Minutes as part of an eight-month investigation into the March 1 attack at the command post, known as Port Shuaiba. The day after the attack, in a press conference, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth insisted the troops there were well-protected.
Iran claims attack on U.S. assets in Bahrain
Iran's military said their forces carried out a drone attack on a U.S. radar system at a base in Bahrain, according to a statement carried by the Iranian state broadcaster on Sunday.
"The U.S. air defense radar system at the Al-Riffa helicopter base in Bahrain was targeted by six drones belonging to the IRGC Aerospace Force," the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said in a statement posted by the state broadcaster on Telegram.
Bahrain's military later said it had intercepted Iranian airstrikes before they hit their targets.
The interior ministry in an X post urged "residents to remain calm, proceed to the nearest safe location, and follow news through official channels for the protection of public safety."
Mossad director is in D.C. for talks, source tells CBS News
Mossad Director Roman Gofman is in Washington for talks, according to a person familiar with the matter.
The talks between the U.S. and Israel's foreign intelligence agency come at a time of great tension with Iran and amid reports that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is seeking a renewal of war with Tehran.
The source did not confirm the subject of the talks, but a source familiar with the matter said that Gofman met with CIA Director John Ratcliffe while in D.C. this week.
Iraqi prime minister sacks officials over providing oil to Iran-backed militias
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi dismissed nine officials on Saturday, following an investigation into allegations of oil smuggling in the Jurf al-Sakher area, a stronghold of the Iran-backed Kataeb Hezbollah group.
"In light of the investigation's findings," Zaidi "ordered that all individuals accused of involvement in oil smuggling operations be referred to the judiciary," his military spokesman Sabah al-Numan said, without identifying the suspects.
The premier "also ordered the dismissal" of nine officials including from the security and oil sectors.
The northern reaches of Iraq has several Shia Muslim militia groups that support Iran, a majority Shia country. The semi-autonomous groups have routinely launched missiles or drones at Middle Eastern countries in opposition to Iran's interests.
The U.S. and Saudi Arabia, a Sunni majority country and regular target of the Iraqi breakaway groups, launched joint strikes on northern Iraqi groups in July.
CBS/AFP
Netanyahu says it's time to remove Iran threat "once and for all"
Invoking Iran's pursuit to rebuild its nuclear program, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Saturday it's time to eliminate the threat from Iran "once and for all" in a speech about forming a new government following a meeting earlier this week with opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot.
"The Iranian regime, which seeks to destroy Israel, is once again working to revive its nuclear program," Netanyahu said, translated from Hebrew. "And let this be clear: This murderous regime, which did not hesitate to murder many thousands of its own people, will not hesitate to use nuclear weapons against us."
"It will do so the moment it manages to resume uranium enrichment and the accelerated development of nuclear weapons," he continued.
Netanyahu said he met with Eisenkot on Thursday, and the meeting "only strengthened my understanding of how essential it is to establish a national unity government at this time."
In last month's election, Netanyahu's Likud party and its allies received 53 seats in the Knesset, short of the 61 needed to form a government and keep him as prime minister. Eisenkot's Yashar party and its allies won 48 seats, while the Arab coalition took 19 seats.
Netanyahu wondered aloud why Eisenkot would potentially side with the Arab coalition to form what he called a "fragile and dangerous government." Netanyahu is clinging to hopes Eisenkot will agree to a deal to establish a majority and cut out the Arab parties, who he has accused of stealing the election. On Saturday, he referred to them as "supporters of terrorism."
"We must remove this existential threat from over our heads once and for all," Netanyahu said, referring to Iran. "A narrow government, or a government that relies on supporters of terrorism, will not be able to achieve this monumental goal. But a national unity government can achieve it in time, thereby ensuring Israel's security for many years to come."
Saudis intercept drones fired by Houthis near Riyadh, southern region
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Iran-backed Houthi militant group said it intercepted and destroyed two drones on Saturday.
The drones were intercepted near Riyadh and over the southern region. The coalition was not more specific about where in the south it had been intercepted. Riyadh, the country's capital, is located in central Saudi Arabia, though hundreds of miles from the Houthis' base of operations in Yemen.
It was a busy week of drone and missile interceptions by the Saudis. The two drones intercepted on Saturday afternoon were the first since one was fired at the eastern, oil-rich region of the country on Thursday. Multiple drones in the east and near Riyadh were interrupted Thursday, while two ballistic missiles were shot down on Wednesday in the western part of Saudi Arabia and three others were shot down near Riyadh, according to the coalition.
Two drones were also intercepted on Wednesday, the coalition said, though one destroyed near Mecca was disavowed by the Houthis, who have said they will not target the holy city.
Multiple drones, ballistic missiles and cruise missiles were also intercepted over different parts of Saudi Arabia on Monday, the same day the coalition said it took out a weapons manufacturing facility in Yemen.
U.N. official urges Iran, U.S. to let fertilizers through Strait of Hormuz
Iran and the United States should "immediately" allow fertilizer shipments through the Strait of Hormuz to ease the crisis in some of the most vulnerable countries, a senior U.N. official said Saturday.
Jorge Moreira da Silva, head of the U.N. Office for Project Services, told the COP31 climate talks in the Turkish resort city of Antalya that the lack of fertilizers could push millions into poverty.
While Iran and the United States are still trying to negotiate an end to the conflict, Moreira da Silva said he had the same message for both countries.
"They should continue their negotiations about the comprehensive deal — but that deal should not avoid an immediate, exceptional, limited, and time-bound solution for the fertilizers," he said.
"Basically what we need is five vessels a day with fertilizers," he added.
Before the conflict, a third of the world's fertilizers passed through the Strait of Hormuz, and since the blockades, their prices had risen by 30%, Moreira da Silva said.
Sudan's finance minister recently told him the price of food there had doubled in six months, he added. In Nepal, they told him that farmers could no longer afford to buy fertilizers.
"So it's very important that we are aware that countries such as Mozambique, Kenya, Sudan, Somalia, Nepal, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka are facing very significant impact," Moreira da Silva said.
The effects of this shortage could be catastrophic, he warned.
Iran says it shot down "Predator" drone for 2nd straight day
Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps claims to have shot down an American MQ-1 "Predator" drone for the second straight day on Saturday.
This was the 17th MQ-1 drone shot down by Iran, according to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, though that number was not possible to verify. The U.S. certainly has lost a number of the drones, however, either to them being shot down or crashing.
The drone was shot down over Iran's Qeshm Island, which is located along the northern coast of the Strait of Hormuz. Like Friday, the strike was credited to Iran's alleged new air defense system.
The U.S. has lost dozens of unmanned aircraft during the war with Iran, according to a congressional report dated Oct. 5. Forty-five MQ-9 Reaper drones have been lost, just through mid-August, while at least three Predator drones were previously destroyed, according to the report.
There were at least 81 manned or unmanned aircraft lost during the war in Iran through early October, according to the report. As of Aug. 1, the losses amounted to a cost of between $1.9 billion and $3.3 billion.
Iran reports 3 incidents of oil tankers hitting mines in Hormuz
Iran's military said on Saturday that fires had broken out on a total of three oil tankers that struck mines in the Strait of Hormuz.
Tehran has insisted vessels obtain its authorization to cross the strait since war erupted with the United States in February, and has attacked ships that do not comply.
"A short while ago, two oil tankers that had switched off their radar and positioning systems and were secretly attempting to transit the Strait of Hormuz through an unauthorized route exploded and caught fire after striking a naval mine," the Revolutionary Guards Corps said in a statement on the incident in the south of the waterway, carried by the Iranian state broadcaster early on Saturday.
A separate statement from Iran's conventional navy said another tanker "navigating through the unsafe and prohibited zone east of the Strait of Hormuz with its tracking and identification systems switched off, caught fire and was forced to stop after striking a naval mine".
The statements did not provide the names or origins of the vessels but the Guards said one of those hit in south Hormuz was a supertanker.
CBS/AFP
Iran say 2 oil tankers struck mines in Strait of Hormuz
Iran's Revolutionary Guards said on Saturday that explosions rang out on two oil tankers after they struck mines in the Strait of Hormuz, where Tehran has restricted navigation.
Since war erupted in February, Tehran has insisted that vessels obtain its authorization to cross the strait and has attacked ships that do not comply.
"A short while ago, two oil tankers that had switched off their radar and positioning systems and were secretly attempting to transit the Strait of Hormuz through an unauthorized route exploded and caught fire after striking a naval mine," the Guards' navy said in a statement carried by an Iranian state broadcaster early on Saturday.
The statement did not provide the names or origins of the vessels, but said one was a supertanker.
The U.S., in response to Tehran's choking of the strategic trade route, has imposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports and provides military support to tankers using the waterway.
In recent weeks, Iran's armed forces have reported several fires or explosions on board ships in the strait, often saying the vessels had struck mines.
On Friday, the Guards released footage of a large plume of smoke rising from a vessel it said was carrying liquefied gas and hit a mine in the south of the strait.
The U.S. military, however, has said it has cleared the main routes through the waterway of mines.
U.N. calls for attacks on civilians in Yemen to stop
U.N. deputy spokesman Farhan Haq said Friday that civilians across Yemen are increasingly being hit by drones, missiles, airstrikes and shelling in their homes, markets and other places once considered safe.
In one of the deadliest attacks since fighting resumed between Iran-backed Houthi rebels and Saudi-backed government forces, at least 30 people died in airstrikes on a market in Taiz province on Nov. 6, according to the Houthis.
Under international law, Haq said all parties must take "all feasible precautions" to avoid and minimize the death and injury to civilians.
Oil prices swing back and forth, wholesale inflation remains high due to diesel costs
Oil prices swung a day after President Trump said the U.S. didn't "need a deal with Iran" even as the conflict in the Middle East drags on.
Brent crude, the international standard, initially jumped early Friday before easing. It was mostly unchanged at $95.89 a barrel at 2 p.m. ET. It was trading near $72 per barrel in late February before the Iran war began.
Rising energy prices because of the U.S. war with Iran have been fueling inflation. Household budgets are getting squeezed directly by higher gasoline costs, but pricier gas and diesel raise costs for anything that is shipped. Prices for everything from food to clothing have been rising.
The latest wholesale inflation report released Friday also shows food prices and other costs gaining ground, despite some easing for energy costs.
CBS/AP
Turkey and Qatar reach a mutual defense agreement
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Qatari Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad al-Thani signed a mutual defense agreement Friday in Istanbul, according to Erdogan's office.
In a statement posted on X, the office said the two sides would continue working together to prevent the resurgence of war in the Gulf region and "persuade the parties to resolve their problems through diplomacy."
There were no further details on the defense agreement between the countries, which already share deep military ties.
The deal follows a joint defense agreement signed between Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia in August in which the three nations pledged to treat an attack on one as an attack on all. Qatar, in its readout of the deal, praised that defense pact and said this one would carry similar weight.
"(The deal has the) aim of strengthening collective defense and promoting regional security and stability, and a unified stance in confronting any external armed attack targeting either party or both of them," Qatar's Ministry of Foreign Affairs said on X.
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan has signaled an openness to other regional countries joining the pact, including Egypt.
Even though Turkey and the Saudis agreed to the defense pact, Turkey has not yet become involved militarily in defending Saudi Arabia from attacks by the Iran-backed Houthi militia in Yemen. Qatar repeatedly came under fire from Iranian attacks during the opening weeks of the U.S.- and Israeli-led war.
CBS/AP
Iran claims to shoot down U.S. MQ-1 "Predator" drone
The Iranian military claimed it shot down a U.S. MQ-1 "Predator" drone near Kuhestak, a city on the coast of the Strait of Hormuz, according to the semi-official ISNA news agency.
The Iranian news outlet shared photos of the supposed downed drone. The U.S. military did not immediately comment on whether one of its drones was shot down.
The Iranian army said its new air defense system was responsible for shooting it down. There have been several confirmed and more claimed shoot-downs of Predator drones in Iran throughout the war.
"We will not hesitate for a moment in safeguarding and defending the territorial integrity, maritime borders and interests of the Islamic Republic of Iran," the Army Public Relations Office said in a statement.
Oil supply surpasses demand for first time since start of war, report says
There was good news in the International Energy Agency's monthly oil report for the first time in awhile: Oil supplies are surpassing demand.
"The oil market is showing tentative signs of rebalancing, with global oil supplies surpassing demand for the first time since the outbreak of the war in Iran," the IEA said in its November report. "Observed oil inventories rose by 52 (million barrels), or 1.7 (million barrels per day), in October as Gulf exports recovered much faster than global oil demand."
The war is still having its effects on the oil market, but the report noted positive movement there as well.
"Despite continued attacks on tankers, Gulf oil exports, excluding Oman, reached 18.4 mb/d last month, 26% below pre-war levels," it said. "The recent increase was led by crude, with flows rising to 15 mb/d, equivalent to 82% of pre-war levels in October."
The good news should continue, the report said.
"Our November supply and demand balances suggest that the global oil market will return to a surplus in 4Q26, with a more substantial build in 2027," it said, before adding the caveat, "As always, downside risks to the forecast persist, as attacks on shipping undermine maritime security, which is pivotal to a sustained recovery."
Much of the increased oil coming out of the Gulf is doing so under U.S. military protection, even as Iran has increased its attacks on oil tankers exiting through the Strait of Hormuz. The U.S. is facilitating ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman, but it is a costly, and for now indefinite, process.
Treasury Secretary Bessent on death threats: "F the Iranian leadership"
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent came out swinging against Iran in the wake of death threats that have caused him to move to a military base for added security.
"F the Iranian leadership," Bessent told CNBC on Friday. "I'm not going to be cowered that they have initiated death threats against me. The other members of the Cabinet are not going to be cowered. And it means what we are doing with Operation Economic Outcast is working."
"The IRGC, they're like a dangerous, cornered animal," he added.
Bessent has come under added threats since the start of a ramped-up sanctions campaign called Operation Economic Outcast in late August, dubbed at the time as "economic D-Day."
Bessent also said the military action undertaken by President Trump was "100% … worth it."
"President Trump took action that had been needed for 47 years, and we'll get on the other side of this," Bessent told CNBC. "Now, President Trump doesn't think we need a deal, and we're just going to keep squeezing them."
Earlier this week, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there was no need to restart military operations in Iran since the economic sanctions were working so well.
U.S. rejects Iranian claim to have hit early warning radar station in Bahrain, says drones intercepted
The U.S. military on Friday denied a claim by Iranian forces to have destroyed a U.S. early-warning radar installation in Bahrain, acknowledging that Iran had launched two attack drones at the small Persian Gulf nation, but saying "both were shot down by U.S. forces."
The claim, attributed to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), was published earlier Friday by various Iranian state media outlets, along with an image said to show the damaged radar station.
In its "Fact Check" post on social media, the U.S. Central Command said there were no injuries or damage caused by the interception of the Iranian drones.
Iran had peppered Bahrain and most other U.S. Gulf allies with daily rocket and drone strikes earlier in the war, but far fewer attacks have been reported since the summer, when major hostilities ended.
U.N. nuclear watchdog "increasingly concerned" about Iran refusing access to underground uranium facility
The United Nations nuclear watchdog agency is "increasingly concerned" about its lack of access to an underground Iranian uranium enrichment facility that Tehran has acknowledged exists, but refused to allow inspectors to visit, according to Reuters.
"The Agency does not know IFEP's exact location, status for safeguards purposes or whether it contains nuclear material," Reuters quoted the International Atomic Energy Agency as saying in a quarterly report to member states, referring to the Isfahan Fuel Enrichment Plant (IFEP).
The IAEA asked Iran to allow inspectors to visit the IFEP in February, but Tehran refused, telling the U.N. agency that "conditions resulting from acts of aggression and the continuation of threats have created a situation in which the normal implementation of safeguards is legally untenable and materially impracticable."
The refusal came after the U.S. and Israel pummeled Iranian nuclear sites, including Isfahan, with a wave of missile strikes in June 2025.
The IAEA said in a September report that, since then, it had observed, in satellite imagery, "regular vehicular activity around the entrance to the tunnel complex at Isfahan," where the agency believes some of the Iran's roughly 900-pound highly-enriched uranium stockpile is believed to have been buried by the June 2025 missile strikes.
"In light of this activity," the IAEA said it requested in February that Iran give inspectors access "as soon as possible," but Tehran has continued to refuse, the nuclear watchdog agency says, citing the attacks on its territory.
The Trump administration has framed Iran's controversial nuclear program as the primary justification for the war, but it has vacillated during the conflict between suggesting Iran would give up its remaining stockpile voluntarily, to declaring the issue largely resolved.
"More than 80 percent of their nuclear industrial base — gone," Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth declared earlier this week," adding: "CRAZY ISLAMISTS IN TEHRAN WILL NEVER EVER HAVE A NUCLEAR WEAPON."
But Iran has agreed to nothing so far regarding its uranium stockpiles or its enrichment program, including renewed IAEA inspections. It has refused to negotiate with the U.S. on the topic until a formal ceasefire is implemented.
On Wednesday, a top Iranian security official insisted Tehran would "not remove even a single particle of enriched nuclear material from the country."
President Trump said Thursday that, "we don't need a deal with Iran," suggesting he may be willing to leave the matter unresolved.
Iran's Revolutionary Guard says it destroyed U.S. radar system in Bahrain
Iran's Revolutionary Guard says it destroyed a U.S. early warning radar in Bahrain, the first such claim in months.
It couldn't be independently verified.
A report by Iran's official IRNA news agency on Friday quoted a statement by the Guard as saying the attack on the U.S. radar system followed a U.S. strike on a telecommunications pole in the southern Iranian port of Sirik.
Bahrain has been one of the strongest critics of Iran and is home to the U.S. Navy's 5th Fleet.
The statement said the attack on the radar was a serious warning to the U.S. to cease its strikes. It was the first report by Iran of targeting a facility in Bahrain since September.
During an air war that began in February, Iran targeted U.S. bases in neighboring Arab nations including Bahrain in retaliation for U.S. strikes. Since then, Iran routinely targets oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, the critical waterway for international oil shipments.
Iran continues to warn ships not to pass through the strategic shipping lane without its approval.
Iran says another ship hit a mine in Strait of Hormuz
Iran's Revolutionary Guard said Friday that there was an explosion on a ship that struck a mine in the Strait of Hormuz, where Tehran has sought to restrict navigation.
Since the outbreak of the Middle East war in late February, Tehran has insisted that vessels obtain its authorization to traverse the strait and has attacked vessels that don't comply.
In response, the United States imposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports and began providing military support to tankers using the vital trade route.
"A few hours ago, a ship carrying liquefied natural gas east of the Strait of Hormuz tried to cross an unauthorized passageway south of the strait, but was hit by a naval mine and exploded violently," the IRGC said on Friday, without giving the name or origin of the vessel.
In recent weeks, Iran's armed forces have repeatedly reported fires or explosions on ships in the strait, often saying they'd hit mines.
The U.S. military, however, claims to have cleared the waterway's routes of mines.
Iran claims U.S. asked Russia to mediate deal
Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf, Iran's chief negotiator, told Al Jazeera that U.S. officials requested that Russian President Vladimir Putin facilitate negotiations between Washington and Tehran.
"It was the Americans who, during a visit to Moscow, spoke with Mr. Putin and asked him to speak with Iran so that, in any case, Iran would agree to speak directly with them," Qalibaf said.
The White House did not directly respond to the Associated Press' query about whether the U.S. had asked Putin to facilitate talks with Iran.
President Trump's senior envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner were in Russia Thursday, where they met Putin to discuss the ongoing war in Ukraine. In their remarks after the meeting, neither Putin nor Mr. Trump's envoys mentioned any discussion about Iran.
-CBS/AP
Trump says "we don't need a deal with Iran," tells Vance to focus on alleged Democratic corruption
President Trump told Vice President JD Vance on Thursday to shift his focus away from the Iran war and instead devote himself to fighting what the president claims is corruption and crime in Democratic-controlled cities and states.
Vance, who served as the lead negotiator for a short-lived truce in the eight-month war, has been blunt in blaming the conflict — and the economic reverberations it has caused — for Republicans' sweeping losses in last week's midterm elections in the United States.
But Mr. Trump brusquely told Vance, in a social media post, to shift his energies away from the Iran war to what he argues is a more pressing - and perhaps more politically salient - issue after Republicans were trounced at the polls.
"We don't need a deal with Iran," Mr. Trump said in the post. "Those days have long since passed. We've got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we've got their Strait!"
Mr. Trump earlier this week said he believed the war "militarily is effectively over," and appeared to double down on that message by pointedly directing Vance "to focus his complete and total attention" on his anti-fraud campaign.
His directive came after The Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday evening that Vance was weighing engaging in a new round of direct talks with a senior Iranian official. The vice president's office did not respond to a request for comment.
-CBS/AP

Iran claims six-drone attack on US air defense radar in Bahrain
MANAMA — Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) claimed Sunday that it had launched six drones targeting a US air defense radar system at a military base in Bahrain, according to Iranian state media.
In a statement broadcast by state-run television and radio, the IRGC said its Aerospace Force had targeted the radar system at the Riffa Helicopter Base in Bahrain.
The IRGC claimed its drones struck the target but provided no independently verified evidence of damage. Neither US nor Bahraini authorities immediately confirmed the reported attack.
The announcement followed two warnings issued by Bahrain's Interior Ministry hours earlier about potential threats, without specifying their nature. The ministry urged residents to remain calm and proceed to the nearest safe location.
In a separate statement carried by Iranian state broadcaster IRIB, the IRGC said the Strait of Hormuz remained closed, citing what it described as Washington's failure to escort ships through the strategic waterway.
It also warned that any further US military action against Iran would be met with a stronger response.
The developments come amid continued tensions between Tehran and Washington over navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, a vital route for global energy and commodity shipments and a central issue in negotiations between the two countries.
The conflict began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28, subsequently spreading across the region. Diplomatic efforts to end the conflict have yet to produce a breakthrough.

Bahrain intercepted and destroyed several Iranian aerial attacks, it said on Sunday, while Tehran said it had struck a US military base in the Gulf kingdom amid uncertainty over a deal to end the US-Israeli war on Iran.
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said it had attacked a US military base in Bahrain in retaliation for "hostile US actions," Iran's Fars news agency reported.
The Revolutionary Guards said they had launched six drones targeting a US air-defense radar at the Al-Rifaa helicopter base in Bahrain, Iranian state-run Press TV reported. There was no immediate confirmation from US or Bahraini authorities.
Bahrain, home to the US Navy's Fifth Fleet, urged citizens and residents to remain calm and proceed to the nearest safe location, the interior ministry said. It did not provide further details on the threats.
Two days earlier the Revolutionary Guards said they had attacked a US early-warning radar in Bahrain. The US military denied this, saying it had intercepted two Iranian drones without any damage.
Diplomatic efforts to end the conflict have yet to produce a breakthrough, though Washington and Tehran have held off on direct attacks in the war that began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28 and then spread across the region, with Tehran launching missile and drone attacks on US bases in Gulf countries.
Trump says he will maintain US naval blockade on Iran
US President Donald Trump has said in recent days that he might hold off on attacking Iran if the US faces no new provocations from Tehran or the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen, but that he would maintain a US naval blockade, Reuters reported on Saturday.
On another front, however, the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition fighting them have continued to exchange attacks, with the coalition saying on Sunday it had intercepted two Houthi ballistic missiles launched towards the Saudi capital Riyadh and three drones in the kingdom's oil-rich Eastern Province.

For Nigerian importers, the cost of replacing a cargo depends on international petrol and diesel quotations, freight, insurance and the naira exchange rate.
A sustained rise in those costs could prompt depot operators to increase the wholesale prices they charge filling stations and other bulk buyers.

Marketers will also weigh local refinery prices and the availability of domestic supplies when deciding what they can afford to pay for their next deliveries.
How higher costs could reach pumps
Any increase at depots would first affect filling stations buying fresh stock. Retailers with fuel purchased at earlier prices may have room to hold their pump prices for longer, while those restocking at higher wholesale rates could adjust sooner. The timing could vary by location and supplier.
Diesel buyers face similar exposure. If wholesale prices rise, businesses that rely on diesel for generators or freight could pay more when they replenish their supplies.

- The Bahrain Defence Force said its air defence systems had thwarted several Iranian aerial attacks.
- The US military has not commented on Sunday’s claim but said it intercepted two Iranian drones on Friday.
MAIN STORY
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has claimed responsibility for launching six drones at a US air defence radar system at Riffa Air Base in Bahrain, escalating tensions between Tehran and Gulf states hosting American military facilities.
The IRGC said the attack was in response to what it described as hostile actions by the United States.
Sirens sounded in Bahrain on Sunday, prompting the country’s Interior Ministry to issue two security alerts within approximately three hours.
The first alert, issued at about 4:30 a.m. local time, warned residents of a potential threat and urged them to remain calm and move to the nearest safe location.
The ministry did not provide further details about the threat.
The Bahrain Defence Force separately said its air defence systems had thwarted several Iranian aerial attacks targeting the kingdom.
The IRGC’s statement, carried by the Fars News Agency, also said the Strait of Hormuz remained closed and claimed that US efforts to escort ships through the waterway had failed.
It warned that any further US attack would attract a stronger response.
The US military has not commented on Sunday’s reported attack.
The latest claim follows another incident on Friday, when the IRGC said it had destroyed a US early-warning radar system in Bahrain.
The Iranian military described that operation as retaliation for what it alleged was an air attack on a telecommunications tower in southern Iran.
However, the US military’s Central Command (CENTCOM) denied that the radar had been destroyed, saying it intercepted two Iranian drones and that there were no injuries or damage.
THE ISSUES
Bahrain’s strategic importance to the United States goes beyond its location in the Gulf. Manama hosts the headquarters of the US Navy’s Fifth Fleet, which oversees American naval operations across the region.
The presence of US military facilities makes Bahrain an important part of Washington’s regional security network, but also exposes the country to risks arising from the confrontation with Iran.
The reported targeting of radar systems is significant because these installations help detect incoming aircraft and missiles, allowing military forces to respond to potential attacks.
The Strait of Hormuz is another major point of concern. The narrow waterway connects the Persian Gulf to international shipping routes and is a critical passage for global oil supplies. Any disruption can affect energy shipments and increase uncertainty in oil markets.
Iran’s claim that the strait remains closed, alongside its warning against US naval operations, adds to concerns about the security of commercial shipping.
WHAT’S NEXT
The US military’s response to Sunday’s reported attack remains outstanding. Its confirmation of intercepting two Iranian drones on Friday contrasts with the IRGC’s claim that it destroyed a US radar system.
Iran has also warned the United Nations Security Council that it would respond immediately to renewed US or Israeli attacks.
Bahrain, meanwhile, has called for the full implementation of Security Council Resolution 2817, which condemned Iranian attacks on Bahrain and other countries in the region and demanded that they stop.
BOTTOM LINE
Iran’s latest drone attack claim puts Bahrain’s security and US military installations in the Gulf back in focus. With Tehran warning against further US action and Washington yet to comment on Sunday’s incident, the risk of renewed confrontation remains a concern for regional security and energy shipping.

sources.news_title: Iran drone strike on Bahrain base reignites Gulf tensions as UK braces for winter energy costs London Journal | The Voice of London
sources.text:
Iran has fired drones at a US radar site in Bahrain for the second time in three days and says the Strait of Hormuz remains closed, a fresh setback for oil markets just as British households face a steep rise in energy bills in January.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said on Sunday that it had launched six drones at a US air defence radar facility at the Riffa air base in Bahrain. Bahrain’s military said its air defences intercepted and destroyed the attack before it could reach its target, according to the BBC.
Sirens sounded across the kingdom and the interior ministry told residents to move to the nearest safe location. Bahrain’s foreign ministry said it “condemns in the strongest terms the continued brutal Iranian attacks on its territory and holds Iran fully responsible for their consequences”.
It was the second Iranian attempt to hit Bahrain in three days. On Friday, Iran fired drones at the Gulf state for the first time since September; the US military said both were shot down and caused no injuries or damage. Saudi Arabia’s foreign ministry has since condemned the latest attack and declared its full solidarity with Manama.
A stand-off over the strait
The strikes come amid a tense stand-off between Washington and Tehran over the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow channel through which about a fifth of the world’s oil and gas normally passes. Shipping has been restricted since the war began in late February, when the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran.
In a statement carried by Iranian state media, the IRGC said: “The Strait of Hormuz is closed, and any aggression by the American enemy will be met with an even harsher and more forceful response.” Tehran describes the Bahrain operation as a reply to what it called the “blatant aggression of the U.S. military”, following US strikes earlier in the week on Iran’s Qeshm Island.
Iran’s Revolutionary Guard navy also said two oil tankers had struck mines and caught fire south of the strait, claiming the ships had switched off their tracking systems and were using an unauthorised route. Those claims have not been independently confirmed.
Diplomacy appears stalled. A preliminary deal reached in June to end the war and reopen the strait collapsed within weeks. This week Donald Trump said the US was no longer interested in a deal and told Vice-President JD Vance to concentrate on domestic politics, although Reuters reported over the weekend that the president was considering holding off on fresh attacks unless provoked.
Iran’s parliamentary speaker, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, said on Sunday that a route to ending the conflict remained open if the US accepted Iran’s “logical conditions”, but warned that Tehran would not stay in a state of “neither war nor peace”, Bloomberg reported.
What it means for UK readers
For households in London and across Britain, the conflict is felt most sharply at the petrol pump and in the energy bill. Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, traded at about $72 a barrel before the war and peaked at $126 at the end of April. It had eased to its lowest level since late August this week, after Mr Trump said the war was “effectively over”, and stood at about $95 on Friday, the Guardian reported. The International Energy Agency said global oil supply returned to surplus in October for the first time since the fighting began.
Renewed attacks in the Gulf threaten that fragile recovery. Diesel is still averaging around 197p a litre, close to October’s record of £2, while petrol has dropped to about 168p, according to the AA. Its fuel price spokesperson, Luke Bosdet, said London and the south-east stood out for having none of the cheaper forecourts found in northern England, Wales and Scotland.
Home energy is the bigger worry. Forecasts from British Gas, EDF and E.ON suggest the typical household bill could rise by more than a quarter in January, roughly £460 a year, with Europe’s winter gas stores at their lowest since records began in 2011, the BBC reported.
What happens next
Traders will be watching how oil prices react as markets reopen this week, and whether the latest Iranian claims about tanker strikes are confirmed. Diplomatically, attention turns to Shenzhen, where the Kremlin says Vladimir Putin, Xi Jinping and Donald Trump will hold a three-way meeting on 19 November on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.
For now, both Washington and Tehran say the door to a settlement is not fully shut. But with drones in the air over Bahrain and mines reported in the strait, British motorists and bill payers may have to wait some time yet for lasting relief.

LAHORE MIRROR (AFP) — Blasts echoed over Bahrain on Sunday as the tiny Gulf nation was rattled by the second Iranian drone attack in three days, ending a long lull in strikes during the Middle East war.

Iran also fired drones at Bahrain on Friday — the first strikes since September against countries in the energy-rich Gulf, which has been heavily targeted in the eight-month war.
Explosions could be heard around 4am (6am PKT) on Sunday, an AFP journalist said, with residents reporting a second series of blasts around 6:30am.
The interior ministry, posting on X, called on “residents to remain calm, proceed to the nearest safe location, and follow news through official channels”.
Mohammed Abdallah, a shopkeeper in the capital, Manama, heard the strikes overnight. “I was hoping this period was behind us and wouldn’t happen again,” he said.
‘Settling scores’
Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said the drones targeted a US radar system at a helicopter base, according to a statement carried by the Iranian state broadcaster.
“The US air defence radar system at the Al-Riffa helicopter base in Bahrain was targeted by six drones belonging to the IRGC Aerospace Force,” the Guards said in a statement posted by the state broadcaster on Telegram.
“The Strait of Hormuz is closed, and any aggression by the American enemy will be met with an even harsher and more forceful response,” it added.
Bahrain “rejects turning its territory into an arena for settling scores and holds Iran fully responsible for these attacks”, a foreign ministry statement said.

The Gulf countries have weathered thousands of Iranian drones and missiles since the war began on February 28.

The US military’s Central Command (Centcom) said it shot down two Iranian drones in Friday’s attack, reporting no casualties or damage.
Centcom, which oversees American military operations in the region, said last month that it had helped Gulf countries export 1.5 billion barrels of oil since the summer via Hormuz.
US President Donald Trump, whose steep reverse in midterm elections was partly blamed on the Iran war, plans to discuss the conflict at a trilateral meeting with his Chinese and Russian counterparts this week, an official said Friday.
